name: Stralsund
title: Ship Thickness Gauging in Stralsund | Coasters and Bulkers
description: Ship thickness gauging in Stralsund for coasters, small bulkers, passenger vessels and workboats: holds, hatch covers, ballast tanks and hull plating alongside.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Coasters and Passenger Vessels in Stralsund
intro: Stralsund faces the island of Rügen across the Strelasund, a narrow, shallow sound that limits the port to coasters, small bulk carriers and the passenger vessels serving Rügen and Hiddensee. Grain from the Pomeranian farmland, timber and building materials keep the quays busy, and harvest brings a seasonal peak. Owners and superintendents use those cargo calls, and the winter lay-up of passenger craft, for thickness gauging. Atlantis has nobody based in Stralsund; the technicians travel from India for each job and join the vessel at its berth.

highlights.p: Once the Pomeranian harvest is in, coasters queue to load grain for Baltic and North Sea buyers. Holds have to be clean and sound before loading, which makes the hours before the first grain goes in a natural moment to gauge hold plating and frames.

Excursion ships and island ferries working from Stralsund in the season are laid up through the winter. With the ship idle, the team can measure bottom and side plating from inside, frames, tanks and piping without disturbing a timetable.

Depth in the sound restricts Stralsund to smaller tonnage. Those ships are often older and under owners who run lean, so a targeted set of readings before a survey is the most useful way to control the steel bill.

port.h: Stralsund: a port on the Strelasund
p: Stralsund sits on the mainland shore of the Strelasund, the strait that separates Rügen from Western Pomerania. The old town, a UNESCO World Heritage site shared with Wismar, comes almost to the water, and the commercial port lies just north of it. Two crossings link the town to Rügen: the older Rügendamm, with its Ziegelgraben bascule bridge that opens at set times for ships passing through the sound, and the high-level Rügen Bridge beside it. Ships reach Stralsund through shallow coastal waters, with marked channels running past the low islands and lagoons of the Western Pomerania Lagoon Area National Park, so the approach rewards local knowledge and limits the size of ship that can come in. Ships bound further south through the sound, towards Greifswald or the Peene, time their passage to the bridge openings.

Cargo traffic suits that setting. Coasters and small bulk carriers load grain from the large farms of the region and carry timber, building materials and agricultural supplies, working at quays a short walk from the old town. Harvest sets the pace: from late summer, grain movements build up, berths are in demand and turnarounds shorten, while the winter months are quieter. Passenger traffic is a large part of the waterfront's life, with ferries and excursion ships running to Rügen, to Hiddensee and around the lagoons in the season, and river and coastal cruise ships visiting in summer. Workboats, survey craft and the dredgers that keep the shallow channels open also use the port, and some of them are based here year-round. Few ships stay long, but most stay long enough for a planned scope.

Shipbuilding shaped modern Stralsund. The Volkswerft on the northern waterfront built fishing vessels, cargo ships and, most recently, a polar expedition cruise ship before the MV Werften group failed in 2022. The city now owns the site as a maritime industrial park. A ship repair company worked in the large building hall from 2023, but its lease ended and it stopped operating in spring 2026, and the hall has since been let to a boatbuilder working on naval training craft. For merchant ships, Stralsund is therefore a cargo port rather than a repair stop, and gauging here is done afloat at the quays or on idle vessels. The site's quays and shiplift remain, and the city has said it wants maritime industry there, so the picture may change again.

facilities.h: Where ships can be gauged in Stralsund
p: Coasters and small bulkers are gauged at the cargo quays during their stay, which may be a day or two for a grain loading. Holds are best measured clean and empty before loading starts, ballast tanks during the call once the crew has emptied and ventilated them. Hatch covers can be measured whenever they are open. Because the ships are small, a single team can often cover a substantial part of a hold or a set of tanks in one call, provided the crew has prepared the spaces and access in advance.

Passenger vessels are a different job. Through the winter they lie at their home berths in the harbour, and an owner preparing for a flag inspection or a slipping can open tanks and bilges and give the team days rather than hours. No yard on the former Volkswerft site was offering merchant ship repair at the time of writing, so docking work goes to yards elsewhere on the German or Polish coast or further afield. Readings taken in Stralsund before that docking let the owner settle the steel scope early. Ships waiting off the port for a berth can be reached by boat for very small scopes.
list: Cargo quays north of the old town — hold, hatch cover and ballast tank gauging on grain, timber and building-materials coasters.
Passenger and excursion berths — bottom, side shell, frame and tank gauging on ferries and excursion ships during winter lay-up.
Workboat and service berths — hull and deck plating on survey craft, dredgers and harbour vessels between assignments.
Lay-by berths in the harbour — pre-purchase and condition gauging on small cargo ships waiting for cargo or for sale.
Docking yards elsewhere on the coast — Stralsund readings passed on so steel renewal is planned before the ship arrives.

context.h: Port state control, small-ship rules and the national park
p: Cargo ships at Stralsund come under German port state control within the Paris MoU, carried out by the Ship Safety Division of BG Verkehr, which also certifies the German-flag passenger vessels that work these waters. Many of the coasters calling here are older ships under European flags, and because the Paris MoU targets ships by age and type, a call at Stralsund can bring an inspection. Hatch covers, air pipes, holds and ballast tanks are where those ships tend to show their age, and gauging records help a superintendent show that each is under control.

The approaches run through and beside a national park, so ships keep to the marked channels and discharges are tightly controlled. EU rules reach even the smallest cargo ships calling here: general cargo vessels from 400 GT have reported emissions under EU MRV since 2025, and ships of every flag calling at the port need an Inventory of Hazardous Materials. In cold winters the shallow sound and lagoons freeze more readily than the open Baltic, which can slow traffic and makes winter the season for work on ships that are already tied up.

jobs.p: Stralsund jobs are small in scale and closely tied to the season. In late summer and autumn, the work is on grain coasters and small bulkers during loading calls, with holds measured clean before the cargo goes in and ballast tanks during the stay. In winter, passenger vessels and workboats in lay-up give longer windows for hull and tank programmes. All year, owners of small cargo ships use Stralsund calls for pre-purchase and pre-survey gauging. Each scope is agreed with the superintendent or owner beforehand, so the most important readings are taken first and nothing essential is left over when the ship sails. Examples:
list: A grain coaster before loading in the harvest season: hold side plating, frames and tank top gauged while the holds are clean and empty.
An excursion ship laid up for the winter: bottom and side shell plating, frames and tank structure gauged from inside ahead of its slipping.
A small bulk carrier carrying building materials: hatch cover panels and coaming tops measured and checked for cracks during discharge.
A dredger or channel-maintenance vessel between contracts: deck, hull and spud-well area gauging to plan repairs.
Pre-purchase gauging of a coaster lying at a lay-by berth: holds, ballast tanks and deck plating measured for the buyer.

logistics: Hamburg and Berlin Brandenburg are the main international airports for Stralsund, both connected by rail to the town's main station; Rostock-Laage, closer, has few international flights. Technicians from India need Schengen visas for Germany, and we plan their travel around the confirmed loading or lay-up dates. The ship's agent or, for passenger vessels, the owner's office arranges harbour access, and for cargo ships confirms that holds and tanks will be emptied and ventilated before the team boards.
vessels: Coasters and short-sea general cargo ships

faqs.q: Is there still a shipyard for repairs in Stralsund?
faqs.a: Not for merchant ship repair at the time of writing. The former Volkswerft site belongs to the city, and the repair company that used its large hall stopped operating in spring 2026; the hall is now let to a boatbuilder. Ships calling at Stralsund dock at yards elsewhere on the German or Polish coast or further afield, and gauging here is done afloat, with readings sent ahead to the docking yard.

faqs.q: When is the best time to gauge a grain coaster at Stralsund?
faqs.a: Before loading, while the holds are clean, dry and empty. The crew can then light the holds and rig access to frames and tank top, and the team measures in the order agreed with the superintendent. During the harvest season turnarounds are short, so we ask for the expected loading date early and fix the scope to fit the time between arrival and the start of loading.

faqs.q: Can you gauge passenger vessels in winter lay-up?
faqs.a: Yes, and winter is the best time. With the ship idle at its home berth, the owner can have tanks emptied and bilges cleaned, and the team can measure bottom and side shell plating, frames, tank boundaries and piping without working around a timetable. The readings help the owner plan plating work before a slipping and answer questions from the flag inspector.

faqs.q: Does ice in the Strelasund stop the work?
faqs.a: Ice can slow shipping in a cold winter, because the shallow sound freezes more readily than open water, but work on a ship already tied up continues. Cold affects deck work and couplant on exposed steel, so outside readings take longer, while work in holds, tanks and engine rooms is little affected. For cargo ships, we confirm the call date with the agent before mobilising if ice is forecast.
